item.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, and collaborators at CMU, Allen Institute for AI, University of Washington, NVIDIA, UC San Diego, and Google Research show that a single frozen large language model (LLM) can act as generator, critic, and rewriter in a prompt-only loop, and that this loop improves outputs across seven generation tasks without any additional training.

Like humans, large language models (LLMs) do not always generate the best output on their first try. Motivated by how humans refine their written text, we introduce Self-Refine, an approach for improving initial outputs from LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The main idea is to generate an initial output using an LLMs; then, the same LLMs provides feedback for its output and uses it to refine itself, iteratively. Self-Refine does not require any supervised training data, additional training, or reinforcement learning, and instead uses a single LLM as the generator, refiner, and feedback provider. We evaluate Self-Refine across 7 diverse tasks, ranging from dialog response generation to mathematical reasoning, using state-of-the-art (GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4) LLMs. Across all evaluated tasks, outputs generated with Self-Refine are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over those generated with the same LLM using conventional one-step generation, improving by ~20% absolute on average in task performance. Our work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 can be further improved at test time using our simple, standalone approach.

Methods

The method is deliberately minimal. Self-Refine takes an input , uses three handcrafted few-shot prompts — p_gen, p_fb, p_refine — and runs the same model three ways: produces the initial output ; emits natural-language feedback on ; and the refine step writes from the model conditioned on the input plus the full history of prior outputs and feedback (). No fine-tuning, no external reward model, no reinforcement learning. The loop halts either at a fixed iteration budget or when itself signals that no further refinement is needed. The paper evaluates on dialogue response generation, code optimization, code readability improvement, mathematical reasoning (GSM8K [5]), sentiment reversal, acronym generation, and constrained generation, with base models GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo), ChatGPT, Codex [6] (code-davinci-002), and GPT-4.

Two things distinguish the prompts from generic “what do you think?” critique prompting. First, p_fb is few-shot-exemplified to elicit feedback that is actionable (names a concrete change to make) and specific (pinpoints the exact phrase or line to change). The Figure 2(e) example — “This code is slow as it uses a for loop… A better approach is to use the formula (n(n+1))/2” — is the template: identify the offending construct, propose the replacement. Second, p_refine is also few-shot, with quadruples that show how to translate feedback into a concrete edit rather than paraphrase or hedge.

The few-shot exemplars in p_fb are themselves built from a per-task rubric — 10 qualitative aspects for Dialogue Response Generation (relevant, informative, interesting, consistent, etc.), a 5-dimension rubric for Acronym Generation (pronunciation, spelling, etc.), the missing-concept checklist for Constrained Generation. The rubric is never invoked explicitly at inference. The model learns it from the exemplars.

Results

Across the seven tasks, Self-Refine beats single-shot prompting by 5–40 points absolute, averaging around 20 points of improvement by human preference and automatic metrics. The gains are largest on tasks with multifaceted or hard-to-define objectives (dialogue, code readability, constrained generation) and smallest on math reasoning, where Table 1 shows essentially no improvement (↑0 to ↑0.2) — the paper attributes this to the feedback model’s inability to detect subtle math errors. Code optimization improves by 8.7 points absolute on GPT-4 (27.3 → 36.0), and by up to 13 points absolute when applied to Codex. Human raters prefer Self-Refine outputs at rates generally consistent with the automatic metrics. The paper releases prompts and code.

The paper also ablates the feedback prompt itself, replacing actionable+specific feedback with generic “what do you think?” feedback or no feedback at all (Table 2). The actionable+specific shape carries most of the signal, especially on tasks where “good output” is hard to define — Sentiment Reversal goes from 43.2 to 31.2 to 0 across the three feedback regimes. On Code Optimization, where “fast” is well-defined, generic feedback already gets you most of the way there.

My Notes

  • The gain doesn’t generalize beyond strong critics. The ~20-point headline held up in the paper’s own benchmarks but is sensitive to task and model. Kamoi et al. [4] [4]’s survey concludes that no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback generated by LLMs prompting themselves under fair settings, and they specifically flag Self-Refine’s evaluation as over-stating the gain (Table 4 of the survey: weak prompts on the initial-response side combined with appropriate prompts on the self-correction side). On reasoning tasks, Huang et al. [2] [2] show intrinsic self-correction can degrade accuracy on average — Table 1’s near-zero math result here was already a tell. The loop assumes the critic produces actionable feedback. When the critic is weak (smaller models make this worse rather than introduce it), the iterations don’t help.
  • Feedback quality drives more gain than iteration count. The paper omits the cleanest ablation: a single-pass critique-and-refine prompt that gives the base LLM the rubric without iteration. Without it, a substantial part of the gain on dialogue and constrained generation may be attributable to the rubric embedded in the feedback prompt rather than to iteration itself. Reflexion [3], which appeared around the same time, makes the memory question explicit: it persists verbal reflections across episodes, while Self-Refine’s history is scoped to a single input.
  • The prompt-only antecedent of o1. Self-Refine spends several times more tokens per problem than one-shot generation in exchange for task-quality gains — the same compute-for-quality tradeoff that o1-style models would later formalize with RL-trained chains, but realized through prompting alone. In 2023 the framing was novel. The test-time compute idiom only entered general usage with the o1 release in late 2024.

item.title: The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Anthropic published the research agenda for The Anthropic Institute (TAI) on May 7, 2026. The premise: a frontier lab can see AI’s real-world effects earlier than outside researchers can, and TAI’s job is to publish those signals so external organizations, governments, and the public can act on them. Outputs are described as inputs to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and to release decisions, with the Anthropic Fellowship as the recruitment surface. The LTBT is an independent five-trustee body that, via a special Class T share, elects a growing share of Anthropic’s board (a majority within four years); its remit was announced as long-range and extreme-event decisions, not day-to-day operations.

The agenda lays out four pillars:

  • Economic diffusion. Higher-cadence and more granular data from the Anthropic Economic Index as an “early warning signal for significant change and disruption”. Open questions:
    • adoption inequality across countries;
    • firm-level concentration of AI usage;
    • productivity growth;
    • how junior-role pipelines train senior practitioners once AI absorbs the entry-level tasks.
  • Threats and resilience. Topics feeding the Frontier Red Team and Project Glasswing backlog, framed by an explicit asymmetric tempo (capabilities advance in months, regulatory and insurance responses on years):
    • dual-use observability;
    • market-based risk pricing;
    • offense-defense balance in cyber and bio;
    • crisis-coordination infrastructure for AI scenarios.
  • AI systems in the wild.
    • group epistemology when most users consult the same few models;
    • critical-thinking degradation under increasing deference;
    • governance of autonomous agents, with naval-law analogies for unattended ships;
    • AI oversight of AI.
  • AI-driven R&D.
    • telemetry for measuring research speedup;
    • “fire drill” tabletop exercises for an intelligence-explosion scenario;
    • who governs systems that build their successors;
    • a separate “jagged frontier” question on whether models can be steered toward high-externality science (drug discovery, materials) that markets underweight.

My Notes

  • TAI is the field’s first research-agenda layer. Across the four frontier labs, OpenAI’s Our principles and its peer documents map two existing document types: declared values and deployment gates. TAI is a third type, set up to produce empirical findings the other two layers can be checked against. The Anthropic Economic Index, with more granular data and higher cadence under TAI, is one concrete commitment. OpenAI’s new “Adaptability” principle commits to updating positions as evidence accumulates; TAI is the closest the field has to an institution set up to produce that evidence.

  • Two ways TAI matters, both untested.

    • Externally, the agenda promises an “early warning signal for significant change and disruption”, language that asserts a verifiable measurement. If outsiders can’t reproduce TAI’s numbers from the published procedure, anyone acting on the early-warning claim has to take Anthropic’s word for it.
    • Internally, TAI’s findings feed into the LTBT, giving the Trust a steady research-policy stream beyond the extreme-event scope it was originally announced for. That integration becomes meaningful only when a Trust position publicly diverges from a commercial decision.

  • The R&D pillar’s telemetry could check Clark’s forecast. Jack Clark put 60% on full AI-driven R&D by end of 2028 from public benchmark trends. TAI commits to publishing the internal R&D speedup data that would let outside readers compare that forecast to actual progress. Without publication, the pillar stays purely internal and only useful to Anthropic.
